citeAs: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach (2019). Towards VQA Models That Can Read. CVPR 2019.
creator: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach (Facebook AI Research, Georgia Institute of Technology)
description: TextVQA is a Visual Question Answering dataset containing 45,336 questions on 28,408 images that require reading and reasoning about text in the image to answer. Images are sourced from Open Images v3 from categories that tend to contain text (e.g., billboard, traffic sign, whiteboard). Each question-image pair has 10 ground truth answers provided by humans.
name: TextVQA
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All 10 annotators agree on the most common answer for 22.8% of questions, while 3 or more annotators agree on the most common answer for 97.9% of questions. Human accuracy on the dataset is 85.01% on validation and 86.79% on test.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline was used. Stage 1: annotators identified images without text (yes/no flag), filtering out images without text. Stage 2: annotators provided 1-2 questions per image requiring reading text to answer; a second question had to differ from the first and have a different answer. Stage 3: 10 answers were collected per question. Annotators were given quality-control options (no text in image, not a question, answer doesn't require reading text, unanswerable), and questions flagged by a majority were removed. Hand-crafted questions with known answers were used to identify and filter bad annotators.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset has low question and image bias: Question Only and Image Only baselines achieve only 8.09% and 6.29% validation accuracy respectively, showing no significant bias w.r.t. images and questions. The most common answer ("yes") is the majority answer for only 4.71% of the dataset, and yes/no questions make up only 5.55% of the dataset. The dataset was collected from sighted humans rather than visually impaired users, unlike the VizWiz dataset.
rai:dataCollection: Images were sourced from Open Images v3, selecting categories likely to contain text (e.g., billboard, traffic sign, whiteboard) by running the Rosetta OCR system on 100 random images per category and using average OCR box count as sampling weights. A three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline collected questions and answers: stage 1 filtered images without text, stage 2 collected questions, and stage 3 collected 10 answers per question.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from Open Images v3 dataset, specifically from categories that tend to contain text such as billboard, traffic sign, and whiteboard.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: 8.9% of TextVQA questions can only be answered by combining multiple OCR tokens, which the model cannot handle. The OCR model fails at detecting text that is rotated, unstructured (e.g., a scribble), or partially occluded. The dataset was collected from sighted humans rather than visually impaired users.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were filtered by running Rosetta OCR on 100 random images per Open Images category to compute average OCR box counts, which were used as per-category sampling weights. In stage 1 of crowdsourcing, annotators flagged images without text, and those images (plus noisy annotator data) were removed, resulting in 28,408 images. Questions flagged by a majority of workers as low quality were also removed.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is motivated by the needs of visually impaired users, for whom reading text in images is a dominant category of questions asked of assistive devices. Progress on this dataset could improve assistive technology for the visually impaired.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking VQA models that can read and reason about text in images; developing assistive technology for visually impaired users; encouraging research on text detection and recognition in unconstrained environments.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Rosetta OCR system was used to identify text-containing images during dataset construction (computing average OCR boxes per category for image sampling weights).

evidence.name: We introduce a new "TextVQA" dataset to facilitate progress on this important problem.
evidence.description: TextVQA contains 45,336 questions on 28,408 images that require reasoning about text to answer. ... It contains 45,336 questions asked by (sighted) humans on 28,408 images from the Open Images dataset [27] from categories that tend to contain text e.g. "billboard", "traffic sign", "whiteboard". Questions in the dataset require reading and reasoning about text in the image. Each question-image pair has 10 ground truth answers provided by humans.

evidence.isLiveDataset: We divide TextVQA into train, validation and test splits with size 34,602, 5,000, and 5,734, respectively.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question-image pair has 10 ground truth answers provided by humans.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We set up a three stage pipeline for crowd-sourcing our data. In the ﬁrst stage, annotators were asked to identify images that did not contain text (using a forced-choice "yes"/"no" ﬂag). ... In the second stage, we collect 1-2 questions for each image. ... Following VQA [3, 10] and VizWiz [13] datasets, we collect 10 answers for each question.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: We use Open Images v3 dataset [27] as the source of our images. ... We run a state-of-the-art OCR model Rosetta [6] on these images and compute the average number of OCR boxes in a category. The average number of OCR boxes per-category were normalized and used as per-category weights for sampling the images from the categories.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: We use Open Images v3 dataset [27] as the source of our images. In line with the goal of developing and studying VQA models that can reason about text, we are most interested in the images that contain text in them. Several categories in Open Images ﬁt this criterion ( e.g., billboard, trafﬁc sign, whiteboard).
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We use Open Images v3 dataset [27] as the source of our images. ... We set up a three stage pipeline for crowd-sourcing our data.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Filtering those (and noisy data from annotators) out resulted in 28,408 images, which form the basis of our TextVQA dataset. ... We remove the questions where a majority of workers marked any of these ﬂags. Additionally, we use hand-crafted questions for which we know the correct answers to identify and ﬁlter out bad annotators.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All 10 annotators agree on the most common answer for 22.8% questions, while 3 or more annotators agree on most common answer for 97.9% questions.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We run a state-of-the-art OCR model Rosetta [6] on these images and compute the average number of OCR boxes in a category. The average number of OCR boxes per-category were normalized and used as per-category weights for sampling the images from the categories.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We believe TextVQA will encourage research both on improving text detection and recognition in unconstrained environments as well as on enabling the VQA models to read and reason about text in images.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Studies have shown that a dominant class of questions asked by visually impaired users on images of their surroundings involves reading text in the image. ... the VizWiz study [5] found that up to 21% of these questions involve reading and reasoning about the text captured in the images of a user's surroundings
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: 8.9% of the TextVQA questions can only be answered by combining multiple OCR tokens; we leave this as future work. ... Our OCR model, while mature, still fails at detecting text that is rotated, a bit unstructured (e.g., a scribble) or partially occluded.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Question only (Q) and Image only (I) baseline get 8.09% and 6.29% validation accuracies, respectively, which shows that the dataset does not have signiﬁcant biases w.r.t. images and questions. ... The most common answer ("yes") is the majority answer for only 4.71% of the dataset and "yes/no" (majority answer) questions in total only make up 5.55% of the dataset.
evidence.datePublished: All top entries in the CVPR VQA Challenges (2016-18) struggle to answer questions in category requiring reading correctly.
